Data Mining Project - Mental Health in Tech Survey¶

Authors: Xiaoyan Li s201292, Maria Porębska s198113, Wiktoria Kopciał s197774¶
Date: 29.04.2025¶

Part I: Problem understanding and Data understanding¶

General Description of the Dataset¶

The Mental Health in Tech Survey dataset is holding the results of the survey conducted in 2014 in order to measure attitudes towards mental health and frequency of mental health disorders in the tech workplace. The survey collected data from respondents worldwide.

Data Mining Goals and Success Criteria¶

Data mining goals:¶

The goal is to understand how certain factors influence mental health and people’s attitude toward it. In particular, we want to analyze how work life impacts mental health. We also aim to predict what kinds of people are more likely to seek mental health treatment and in which countries the organizations are the most opened to discussing mental health issues.

Succes criteria:¶

Success will be measured by the ability:

  • to find at least 5 statistically significant patterns (p < 0.05) in the data (which factors are associated with mental health outcomes or attitudes);
  • to build a prediction model for treatment-seeking behavior that achieves an accuracy of at least 70%;
  • to identify significant country-level differences in mental health openness with at least 3 countries showing statistically significant variance (p < 0.05)

Characteristics of the Dataset¶

Original Dataset is taken from Open Sourcing Mental Illness and survey responses can be viewed here.
The survey collected 1260 responses.
The dataset consists of one set that can be viewed in two formats:

  • CSV under at the kaggle website
  • Excel file from Open Sourcing Mental Illness.

Description of the Attributes¶

(Name - Type; Meaning; Unit of Measurement; Special Values)

"A little about you" section

  • Timestamp - Date; Day, month and year of response submission; Date in a calendar; -
  • Age - Numerical (Integer); Respondent Age; Years; Negative values or very Big values that could indicate an error
  • Gender - Nominal (string); Respondent gender; None ;Special Values include: typos (eg.mail), "prefer not to say" type responses(eg.Nah), identifying with multiple genders (eg.she/they), using only first letter (eg.m/f), synonyms of male/female/non-binary (eg.Guy), longer descriptions or clarifications (eg.ostensibly male, unsure what that really means; Female (trans))
  • Country - Nominal (string); Respondent country; None; Unusual territories (eg.Bassas da India, Europa Island, Giblartar)
  • state - Nominal (string), respondent state or territory (if they live in United States) (abbrivitations of states); None; missing values for respondents living elsewhere
  • self-employed - Nominal, Binary (yes/no); whether the respondent is self-employed; None; missing values
  • family_history - Nominal, Binary (yes/no); whether the respondent has a history of mental-illness in their family; None; -
  • treatment - Nominal, Binary (yes/no); whether the respondent has sought treatment for a mendal health condition; None; -
  • work_interfere - Ordinal (Often - Never scale); Whether the respondent feels that their mental health condition (if they have one) interferes with their work, and to what extent, how often; None; missing values (no mental health condition)

"Where you work" section

  • no_employees - Ordinal (string); The number of employees in the respondent's company or organization (in ranges); None; -
  • remote_work - Nominal, Binary (yes/no); whether the respondent works remotely (outside of an office) at least 50% of the time; None; -
  • tech_company - Nominal, Binary (yes/no); whether the respondent's employer is primarily a tech company/organization; None; -
  • benefits - Nominal (yes/no/don't know); whether the respoondent's employer provide mental health benefits; None; -
  • care_options - Nominal (yes/no/not sure); whether the respondent knows the options for mental health care their employer provides; None; -
  • wellness_program - Nominal (yes/no/don't know); whether the respondent's employer has ever discussed mental health as part of an employee wellness program; None; -
  • seek_help - Nominal (yes/no/don't know); whether the respondent's employer provide resources to learn more about mental health issues and how to seek help; None; -
  • anonymity - Nominal (yes/no/don't know); whether the respondent's anonymity is protected if they choose to take advantage of mental health or substance abuse; None; -
  • leave - Ordinal (very easy - very difficult scale, don't know); whether it is easy for the respondent to take medical leave for a mental health condition; None; -

"Openness about mental health" section

  • mental_health_consequence - Nominal (yes/no/maybe); whether the respondent thinks that discussing a mental health issue with their employer would have negative consequences; None; -
  • phys_health_consequence - Nominal (yes/no/maybe); whether the respondent thinks that discussing a physical health issue with your employer would have negative consequences; None; -
  • coworkers - Nominal (yes/no/some of them); whether the respondent would be willing to discuss a mental health issue with their coworkers; None; -
  • supervisor - Nominal (yes/no/some of them); whether the respondent would be willing to discuss a mental health issue with their direct supervisor(s); None; -
  • mental_health_interview - Nominal (yes/no/maybe); whether the respondent would bring up a mental health issue with a potential employer in an interview; None; -
  • phys_health_interview - Nominal (yes/no/maybe); whether the respondent would bring up a physical health issue with a potential employer in an interview; None; -
  • mental_vs_physical - Nominal (yes/no/don't know); whether the respondent feels that their employer takes mental health as seriously as physical health; None; -
  • obs_consequence - Nominal, Binary(yes/no); whether the respondent has heard of or observed negative consequences for coworkers with mental health conditions in their workplace; None; -

"Additional Comments" section

  • comments - Text, open-ended response; additional notes or comments from respondents about their experiences or opinions on mental health topics; None; missing values

# Function to plot countplots for categorical features
def plot_count(feature, title, rotation=0):
    plt.figure(figsize=(10,5))
    sns.countplot(data=df, x=feature, order=df[feature].value_counts().index)
    plt.title(title)
    plt.xticks(rotation=rotation)
    plt.show()
In [ ]:
# Function to plot count plots and percentages for categorical features
def plot_count_with_percentage(feature, title, rotation=0):
    plt.figure(figsize=(10,5))
    gender_counts = df[feature].value_counts()
    sns.countplot(data=df, x=feature, order=gender_counts.index)

    # Add percentages on top of the bars
    total = len(df)
    for p in plt.gca().patches:
        height = p.get_height()
        percentage = (height / total) * 100
        plt.gca().text(p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2., height + 10, f'{percentage:.1f}%',
                       ha='center', fontsize=12, color='black')

    plt.title(title)
    plt.xticks(rotation=rotation)
    plt.show()

In Russia we have mandatory medical insurance. Every employer must pay 3.6% of every employee's salary to the insurance fund like a tax. Everyone gets free healthcare at public clinics and hospitals. Some types of healthcare including mental health are still funded from the government budget but that doesn't matter it's still FREE!However this is Russia :D I don't know much about what actually happens in mental hospitals here except that a lot of young people with male in their passports use these to avoid military draft and doctors seem to help them.

In my previous workplace which had mental health protections policies and access to counsellors my Director went so far as to say to me in somewhat casual conversation A woman was murdered across the street. I have even less faith that a workplace without the policies in place could appropriately handle mental health. I can only imagine it's worse in full tech environments.

I've seen negative consequences towards mental health conditions in previous workplaces.Working remote is empowering in this way.

I'm not a permanent employee so do not get they benefits they get.My client is extremely supportive of permanent staff with mental health issues.

A close family member of mine struggles with mental health so I try not to stigmatize it. My employers/coworkers also seem compassionate toward any kind of health or family needs.

Too many people even especially IT considered mental health issues as a choice or something people can freely act about. You are depressed: take vacation. You feel weird: admit it is physical (otherwise it is not serious) go and see a doctor (and if you are on sick leave too many days you will get fired). You don't feel good today: take a holiday but don't work from home. In startup there is what I call the tyranny of happiness: you have to look happy to be accepted and to be worked with. At some point playing a role can definitely make the mental health issue worse and it is also a threat to diversity :(I don't like to call mental health issues an issue but actually when it comes to company field it too often becomes an issue and this is sad because working is sometimes better than medication. It is a vicious circle: people are scared of speaking about it so they don't inform their coworkers about what mental health is for real and so coworkers are so scared on a regular basis that the people with mental health issues keep it for themselves.

Would you bring up a mental health issue with a potential employer in an interview?Poignant.

I found it difficult to answer all of the questions effectively as many of them would depend on the nature of the mental health issues as some seem more socially accepted than others. For some people telling your current supervisor that you have a history of bi-polar disorder might be easier than telling a potential employer that you have a history of compulsive gambling. They might both be bits of irrelevant information (past behavior and not indicators of future behavior). However western culture pushes us to appear as capable as possible to our supervisors in pursuit of excellence in our work. Providing information that could create a negative bias seems like a more genuine and yet more risky approach to the discussion.

I answered based on previous job at large technical company where I was pushed out of my role within 3 months of disclosing diagnosis.I had been struggling for 3 months prior to disclosure and was incredibly relieved when finally diagnosed. Growing up in a family open about mental health and also at the end of my rope I immediately shared with management what was going on. I requested a temporary reduced workload so I could reduce anxiety. (At time I didn't know it was anxiety as took me a year to accept that the (to me) deserved stress was anxiety caused by my core diagnosis.) When disclosing I didn't deeply understand details of the state of my mental health; I simply knew I was so stressed out by having been unable to get myself to do work in three months that I couldn't juggle all that was currently on my plate.It was at this point my direct manager and I began an almost daily struggle. After working on a single project and making progress (compared to 3 months before diagnosis when management didn't even know how bad I was doing) I requested increasing my workload. This was never granted; boss said I hadn't proved myself and implied I could not be trusted.Two huge issues stick out to me from that experience:1) Company assumes things would be better and back to 100% within months. They did not understand what one goes through when figuring out meds: things at times got worse. They did not understand how long it takes until meds are figured out: mine took two years. They most certainly would not truly understand why to this day four years later despite being stable I'm in counseling every other week in addition to being on meds. Rather than supporting that it would be seen as oh I'm sorry. I was a problem to my manager because he didn't see improvements each week.2) Accomodations.- There was no option for me to reduce work temporarily to part-time (too complicated). Instead they pushed me to take disability leave. I told them that wouldn't help; they told me to double-check with care providers. That required me to see a psychologist unnecessarily as psychologist said I didn't qualify for leave. (Expensive unnecessary appointment).- The assistance I needed the most at work was understanding: I was open but my manager told me to not tell my co-worker assigned to support me. That was disasterous for colleague's stress/frustration levels. He knew something was up but was barred from asking and I was implied it was better to keep my mouth shut.- Accommodations weren't understood by even Benefits as they're not trained in mental health nor do they have people come in to assess how they're doing in supporting those with mental health issues. Should be no different than people coming in to assess for physical accessibility of the workplace. When in a meeting with my manager supervised by HR I shouldn't feel like I'm asking too much of manager when requesting he put the negative critiques on the back burner and help me figure out whether I'm doing anything right. That this didn't stop him from coming into my office that same day and putting on my dick hat to yell at me for something that wasn't even my fault (he had brought in co-worker for this yelling and turned to finish yelling at this person): FUCKING UNACCEPTABLE.While I will never return to that company and as such took the severance package I will NEVER agree with their legal reason for being unable to do the job: me being medically disqualified from this role. I was too expensive in the short term for them; I'm not worth the cost.

I worked too much had too much pressure on myself from being the sole developer on a delayed project that seemed to grow in size with each week it was delayed by and worried about money a lot.I became depressed and anxious and had trouble eating sleeping and generally being myself. As my depression worsened I was regularly late for work couldn't perform as well as I should and became irritable with my colleagues.My employers response after a while was to send me private messages complaining about my lateness which only worsened the situation. I was prescribed 3 weeks off work by my doctor which my employer agreed to only to come back after to find I had been on 'statutory pay' which was roughly half of what I was expecting and was not enough to cover my rent bills AND food. This made me worse and sent me into another depression until I eventually admitted defeat gave up working and left the company. It took me months to recover and I'm now left (over 6 months after this all started) recovering from the fallout I created leaving employment with hardly any money to my name.I had previously been told by my employer that I was too young to burn out and (stupidly) trusted them. I did not feel comfortable discussing my problems with my employer because each time I was met with an attitude that I had to get myself together and ultimately given the amount of employees before me who had left the company by being fired after an altercation with the employer left me with no option but to hide it from them so I too wouldn't be fired.

Correlations Between Attribute Values¶

This section presents chosen correlations between attributes along with short interpretation of the results.

In [ ]:
# functions for fast interpretation of the results
def check_corr_results_point_biserial(statistic, pvalue):
    print('Based on correlation coefficient ')
    if statistic < 0:
        print("there is a negative corelation between variables.")
    elif statistic > 0:
        print("there is a positive corelation between variables.")
    else:
        print("there is no corelation between variables.")

    print('Based on p value with significance level 0.05 ')
    if pvalue > 0.05:
        print("we cannot reject null hypothesis - there is no corelation between variables.")
    else:
        print("we can reject null hypothesis - there is corelation between variables.")

    print("Strength of the correlation: ")
    if abs(statistic) >= 0 and abs(statistic) < 0.1:
        print("no correlation.")
    elif abs(statistic) >= 0.1 and abs(statistic) < 0.3:
        print("little correlation.")
    elif abs(statistic) >= 0.3 and abs(statistic) < 0.5:
        print("medium correlation.")
    elif abs(statistic) >= 0.5 and abs(statistic) < 0.7:
        print("high correlation.")
    else:
        print("very high correlation.")

def check_corr_results_cramers_v(statistic):
    print("Strength of the correlation: ")
    if abs(statistic) >= 0 and abs(statistic) < 0.1:
        print("no correlation.")
    elif abs(statistic) >= 0.1 and abs(statistic) < 0.3:
        print("little correlation.")
    elif abs(statistic) >= 0.3 and abs(statistic) < 0.5:
        print("medium correlation.")
    elif abs(statistic) >= 0.5 and abs(statistic) < 0.7:
        print("high correlation.")
    else:
        print("very high correlation.")

# function for calculating Cramer's V
def cramers_v(var1, var2):
    contingency_table = pd.crosstab(var1, var2)
    chi, pvalue, deg_f, freq = stats.chi2_contingency(contingency_table)
    n = df.shape[0]
    min_val = np.min(contingency_table.shape)-1
    cramers_v = np.sqrt((chi/n)/min_val)
    return cramers_v

Correlation between age and treatment attributes¶

In [ ]:
# Boxplot of Age (cleaned) and Treatment variables
sns.boxplot(x='Age_cleaned', y='treatment', data=df)
plt.title("Age vs Mental Health Treatment")
plt.xlabel('Age')
plt.ylabel('Mental Health Treatment')
plt.show()

# Since Age is numberical/quantitative and Treatment is dichotomous - Apply Point-Biserial Correlation
df['treatment_bin'] = df['treatment'].map({'Yes':1, 'No':0})
stat, pvalue = stats.pointbiserialr(df['treatment_bin'], df['Age_cleaned'])
print('Point-Biserial Correlation statistics: ' + str(stat) + ' p value: ' + str(pvalue))
check_corr_results_point_biserial(stat, pvalue)

no correlation.

Interpretation:¶

Point-Biserial correlation was chosen because age is a quantitative variable and treatment is a dichotomous variable (only Yes and No responses).
Based on the results the correlation is very weak and because statistics is very low, it is safe to state that there is no correlation between age and treatment variables.

Matrix and Heatmap of other correlations of chosen attributes¶

Note: Cells where correlation between the same attribute should be calculated is set to 0 in order to avoid disruptance in the heatmap.
Cramer's V is chosen for calculations because only categorical attributes will be taken into account.

In [ ]:
# variables worth checking for cramer's v correlation matrix:

col = ['Age_Group', 'Gender_cleaned', 'Country', 'state', 'self_employed', 'family_history', 'treatment', 'work_interfere', 'no_employees', 'remote_work', 'tech_company', 'benefits',
       'care_options', 'wellness_program', 'seek_help', 'anonymity', 'leave', 'mental_health_consequence', 'phys_health_consequence', 'coworkers', 'supervisor',
       'mental_health_interview', 'phys_health_interview', 'mental_vs_physical', 'obs_consequence']

cramers_v_matrix = pd.DataFrame(np.zeros((len(col), len(col))), columns=col, index=col)

for col1 in col:
    for col2 in col:
        if col2 != col1:
            cramers_v_matrix.loc[col1, col2] = cramers_v(df[col1], df[col2])
print("Cramer's V results: ")
display(cramers_v_matrix)

sns.heatmap(cramers_v_matrix, cmap='coolwarm')
plt.title("Cramer's V results Heatmap")

Interpretation¶

There is a visible trend for companies with over 1000 employees to offer mental health benefits and provide resources for seeking help for mental health.

In contrast, small and medium enterprises (SMEs) between 6 to 100 people tend not to offer mental health benefits or don't provide resources for seeking help for mental health. Employers of those companies are also less likely to talk about mental health during wellness programs. This could be due to lack of those programs or lower frequency of organising such events. Additionally looking at the plot of treatment and no_employees attributes, one may even think that there is no correlation at all. It is noticable that employees of small companies (6-25 employees) tend not to seek treatment for mental health. This could mean that such wellness programs are either not so much needed/brought-up in small companies.
More respondents working in small companies (1-5 employees) are self employed. Most respondents are not self employed and work for larger companies.

Preliminary findings about the contents of the dataset¶

The findings indicate notable trends in how mental health treatment, company size, and workplace support are related. Larger companies tend to offer more mental health resources, while small companies are less likely to provide support. Gender and family history play a role in treatment-seeking behavior, and cultural factors, such as the perception of mental health as a taboo topic, impact discussions in the workplace.

Data Quality¶

Missing Data & Outliers & Values of Unknown Meaning¶

The dataset has missing values for the following attributes: state, self-employed, work_interfere and comments.

State: The missing values obviously appear in the dataset due to the fact that some people don't live in the U.S., so we counted the amount of people living elswhere and compared it to number of missing values. For people living outside of U.S, we swapped the NaN values to "Not living in U.S", for additional respondents, who live in U.S, but didn't specify their state, we decided to change the missing values to "Unknown state".

Self-employed: Here we also keep missing values, but just change them to "Unknown", because we can't verify the reason why some respondents skip this question.

Work_interfere: Here we keep missing values, but change them to "Not applicable/Unknown", because we assume that most respondents skip this question since they don't have a mental health condition (Not applicable), but we can't check if that's the reason for all respondents (Unknown).

Comments: We drop all the missing comments as we only want to analyze the responses that include some text.

The dataset also has some noticeable outliers, especially in the Age and Gender attributes during the analysis.

Age: The outliers are extreme values that fall outside the expected range of ages, such as negative values, positive yet very small values or values greater than 100 years. These outliers may indicate data entry errors or respondents who either don't fit the profile of the target population (e.g., age values like 5 or 8) or they don't want to disclose this information.

It is essential to address these outliers because they can skew the analysis, especially when calculating averages or distributions. We chose to clean the Age attribute by filtering for realistic values (ages between 18 and 100), leaving only valid data for further analysis.

Gender: There are a few instances of inconsistent or potentially erroneous entries. For example, in the Gender column, values like "M", "F", "mail" (a typo for "male"), and various capitalizations of "male" and "female" were found. These inconsistencies were addressed by standardizing the Gender values to a consistent set of categories: "male", "female", and "other". Such standardization is crucial for ensuring that categorical variables are properly grouped and analyzed.

Overall Data Integrity¶

Overall, the dataset has good data integrity — most variables contain expected values and formats, with only some missing values and a few outliers.

However, there are notable biases affecting data quality and representativeness:

Participation Bias: As an open, voluntary survey hosted by a mental health advocacy group, it likely attracts respondents with personal mental health experiences (78.98% of the responses claimed to have a mental illness based on the 9th variable: work_interfere; 23.1% according to the US National Institute of Mental Health).

Demographic Skew: The data leans U.S.-centric (59.6%), with an overrepresentation of men (77.6%) and individuals aged 18-45 (99.5%).

Limited Applicability: Certain questions don't apply to self-employed individuals or entrepreneurs, who lack traditional supervisors, HR, or organizational support structures.

Cultural Context Bias: Many questions reflect a U.S.-centric view, assuming employer involvement in healthcare, which doesn't align with countries where mental health services are handled by national healthcare systems.

Conclusion

While not representative of the general or global tech population, the dataset still provides valuable insights into the experiences of a self-selected group within a specific cultural and professional context. Despite its biases, meaningful patterns and insights can still be uncovered through careful analysis and data mining within its limitations.

Validity of Data Mining Goals¶

The goals we set are valid because the dataset contains rich information about demographics, workplace characteristics, and mental health attitudes. This enables meaningful analysis of how work life impacts mental health.

Most of the attributes are nominal or ordinal, which are suitable for identifying patterns and building predictive models. Additionally, the presence of country information allows for comparative analysis between countries regarding openness to mental health discussions.

Therefore, the goals are achievable based on the available data.
